note.question: How can a pay-as-you-go provider give poor households genuine payment flexibility without encouraging strategic underpayment or destroying the provider's viability?
note.overview: A PAYGo firm commits to a history-dependent dynamic contract while a forward-looking consumer privately observes disposable income and strategically chooses each payment. The mechanism must make the intended payment policy sequentially optimal and satisfy promise keeping. The paper solves this repeated principal-agent game by recursive contracting and incentive compatibility.

The consumer privately observes current disposable income and chooses how much to pay versus consume. Preferences, income distributions elicited at onboarding, contract terms, and termination payoffs are common knowledge.

components.label: Solution or estimation method
components.explanation: The authors use the promised-utility approach to convert the history-dependent sequential game into a Markovian dynamic program. They solve backward within each period—termination, access, and payment incentives—and then backward across periods, proving concavity of the continuation functions. A numerical PAYGo example illustrates the optimal rules, which are distilled into a simpler points-and-tiers contract.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: At t=0 the firm offers a committed contract, charges a downpayment d, and the consumer accepts only if affordable and individually rational. In each period t=1,...,T, disposable income y_t is privately realized; the consumer chooses payment p_t within the liquidity constraint and consumes the remainder. Based only on payment history, the contract grants fractional access f_t and then randomizes, if prescribed, among confiscation, ownership transfer, and continuation. If continued, a promised future value carries the history into the next period; otherwise terminal payoffs are realized.
